sections.heading: Part I — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Foundational Fluency (1–7)

questions.q: The data set $23,25,31,34,34,38,42,45$ is to be shown as a stem-and-leaf diagram with stems $2,3,4$. Write out the diagram, and use it to find the median.
questions.answer: Stem-and-leaf: $2\mid3\,5$; $3\mid1\,4\,4\,8$; $4\mid2\,5$ (key: $2\mid3=23$). With 8 values, the median is the average of the 4th and 5th values: $34$ and $34$, so median $=34$.
questions.explanation: Stem-and-leaf: $2\mid3\,5$; $3\mid1\,4\,4\,8$; $4\mid2\,5$ (key: $2\mid3=23$). With 8 values, the median is the average of the 4th and 5th values: $34$ and $34$, so median $=34$.

The bar chart shows the number of books read by students in a reading challenge, grouped by number of books. Find the total number of students, and the modal group.
questions.target: Reading grouped frequency data from a bar chart
questions.answer: Total students $=12+28+15+5=60$. The modal group (highest bar) is $3\mathrm{-}5$ books, with 28 students.
questions.explanation: Total students $=12+28+15+5=60$. The modal group (highest bar) is $3\mathrm{-}5$ books, with 28 students.

questions.q: Using the same reading-challenge data (0-2: 12, 3-5: 28, 6-8: 15, 9-11: 5 students), find what percent of students read 6 or more books.
questions.target: Reading grouped frequency data from a bar chart
questions.answer: Students reading 6 or more books: $15+5=20$. Percent of the total 60 students: $\frac{20}{60}\times100\%\approx33.3\%$.
questions.explanation: Students reading 6 or more books: $15+5=20$. Percent of the total 60 students: $\frac{20}{60}\times100\%\approx33.3\%$.

questions.q: A data set has minimum $=8$, $Q_1=15$, median $=22$, $Q_3=30$, and maximum $=40$. State the interquartile range, and determine whether a value of $45$ would be considered an outlier if outliers are defined as values beyond $Q_3+1.5\times IQR$.
questions.answer: $IQR=Q_3-Q_1=30-15=15$. Upper outlier boundary: $Q_3+1.5(IQR)=30+22.5=52.5$. Since $45<52.5$, the value $45$ would NOT be considered an outlier.
questions.explanation: $IQR=Q_3-Q_1=30-15=15$. Upper outlier boundary: $Q_3+1.5(IQR)=30+22.5=52.5$. Since $45<52.5$, the value $45$ would NOT be considered an outlier.

questions.q: A data set has minimum $=5$, $Q_1=12$, median $=18$, $Q_3=27$, and maximum $=50$. State the interquartile range, and determine whether the maximum value would be considered an outlier if outliers are defined as values beyond $Q_3+1.5\times IQR$.
questions.answer: $IQR=Q_3-Q_1=27-12=15$. Upper outlier boundary: $Q_3+1.5(IQR)=27+22.5=49.5$. Since the maximum value $50>49.5$, it WOULD be considered an outlier.
questions.explanation: $IQR=Q_3-Q_1=27-12=15$. Upper outlier boundary: $Q_3+1.5(IQR)=27+22.5=49.5$. Since the maximum value $50>49.5$, it WOULD be considered an outlier.

A data set has mean $=42$, median $=38$, and mode $=35$. Describe the skewness of the distribution.
questions.answer: Since mean $>$ median $>$ mode, the distribution is positively skewed (skewed to the right), with a longer tail of higher values pulling the mean above the median.
questions.explanation: Since mean $>$ median $>$ mode, the distribution is positively skewed (skewed to the right), with a longer tail of higher values pulling the mean above the median.

sections.heading: Part III — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Challenging & Cross-Lesson Synthesis (15–20)

questions.q: Two classes take the same test. Class A has mean $68$ and standard deviation $5$. Class B has mean $71$ and standard deviation $12$. Compare the two classes' performance and consistency.
questions.answer: Class B has a higher mean score (71 vs. 68), so on average Class B performed better. However, Class A has a much smaller standard deviation (5 vs. 12), meaning Class A's scores were more consistent/less spread out than Class B's.
questions.explanation: Class B has a higher mean score (71 vs. 68), so on average Class B performed better. However, Class A has a much smaller standard deviation (5 vs. 12), meaning Class A's scores were more consistent/less spread out than Class B's.

questions.q: Two machines fill bottles with a target volume of 500 mL. Machine X has mean fill volume $500$ mL and standard deviation $2$ mL. Machine Y has mean fill volume $498$ mL and standard deviation $8$ mL. Compare the two machines' accuracy and consistency.
questions.answer: Machine X's mean (500 mL) matches the target exactly, while Machine Y's mean (498 mL) is 2 mL below target. Machine X also has a much smaller standard deviation (2 mL vs. 8 mL), meaning its fill volumes are far more consistent. Machine X is therefore both more accurate and more consistent than Machine Y.
questions.explanation: Machine X's mean (500 mL) matches the target exactly, while Machine Y's mean (498 mL) is 2 mL below target. Machine X also has a much smaller standard deviation (2 mL vs. 8 mL), meaning its fill volumes are far more consistent. Machine X is therefore both more accurate and more consistent than Machine Y.

questions.q: This question has two parts. A delivery company records the delivery times (in minutes) for 50 packages: mean $=34$ minutes, standard deviation $=6$ minutes. Company policy states any delivery beyond 2 standard deviations above the mean is classified as late. (a) Find the delivery-time threshold, in minutes, above which a delivery is classified as late. (b) If a customer's package took 44 minutes to deliver, determine, using the standard deviation, whether this delivery should be classified as late, and state how many standard deviations from the mean this value lies.
questions.target: A well-designed word problem: analyzing delivery times
questions.answer: (a) Threshold $=34+2(6)=34+12=46$ minutes. (b) $44$ minutes is $\frac{44-34}{6}=\frac{10}{6}\approx1.67$ standard deviations above the mean. Since $1.67<2$, this delivery is NOT classified as late.
questions.explanation: (a) Threshold $=34+2(6)=34+12=46$ minutes. (b) $44$ minutes is $\frac{44-34}{6}=\frac{10}{6}\approx1.67$ standard deviations above the mean. Since $1.67<2$, this delivery is NOT classified as late.

questions.q: In an ordered stem-and-leaf diagram of 15 test scores, the key states $3 \mid 5 = 35$. The leaves for stem 4 are $1, 3, 5, 8, 8$. What is the median score if there are 4 scores below stem 4?
questions.answer: For $n = 15$, the median is the 8th value: 4 values are in stem 3, so in stem 4 we count the 5th, 6th, 7th, 8th values (1, 3, 5, 8). The 8th value is 45.
questions.explanation: For $n = 15$, the median is the 8th value: 4 values are in stem 3, so in stem 4 we count the 5th, 6th, 7th, 8th values (1, 3, 5, 8). The 8th value is 45.

questions.q: A data set has minimum $= 12$, $Q_1 = 20$, median $= 28$, $Q_3 = 36$, and maximum $= 52$. What is the interquartile range (IQR)?
Using the $1.5 \times \mathrm{IQR}$ rule on the data from the previous question, determine if the maximum value 52 is an outlier.
choices: No, the upper outlier boundary is 60
Yes, any value above 48 is an outlier
Yes, any value above 50 is an outlier
No, because the range is less than 50
questions.answer: $\mathrm{Boundary} = Q_3 + 1.5 \times \mathrm{IQR} = 36 + 1.5(16) = 36 + 24 = 60$. Since $52 \leq 60$, it is not an outlier.
questions.explanation: $\mathrm{Boundary} = Q_3 + 1.5 \times \mathrm{IQR} = 36 + 1.5(16) = 36 + 24 = 60$. Since $52 \leq 60$, it is not an outlier.

questions.q: In a histogram, the class interval $20 \leq x < 35$ has a frequency of 45. What is the frequency density for this bar?
On a histogram, a bar representing the interval $10 \leq x < 20$ has a width of 2 cm and a height of 5 cm, representing 30 items. What area represents 1 item?
questions.answer: Area of bar $= 2 \times 5 = 10\mathrm{\ cm}^2$. Since this represents 30 items, each item is represented by $10/30 = 1/3\mathrm{\ cm}^2$.
questions.explanation: Area of bar $= 2 \times 5 = 10\mathrm{\ cm}^2$. Since this represents 30 items, each item is represented by $10/30 = 1/3\mathrm{\ cm}^2$.

questions.q: Why is frequency density, rather than raw frequency, plotted on the vertical axis of a histogram for grouped continuous data?
choices: Because class widths may be unequal and area must be proportional to frequency
Because continuous data cannot be plotted with integer frequencies
To ensure the total height of all bars equals 100
To eliminate the need for class boundaries
questions.answer: When classes have unequal widths, plotting frequency density ensures that the area of each rectangle is directly proportional to the frequency of that class.
questions.explanation: When classes have unequal widths, plotting frequency density ensures that the area of each rectangle is directly proportional to the frequency of that class.

questions.q: When plotting a cumulative frequency graph for grouped continuous data, at which points should the cumulative frequencies be plotted?
choices: At the midpoints of each class
questions.answer: Cumulative frequency represents the total number of observations up to that value, so it must be plotted at the upper boundary of each class interval.
questions.explanation: Cumulative frequency represents the total number of observations up to that value, so it must be plotted at the upper boundary of each class interval.

questions.q: From a cumulative frequency curve of 200 students, the 80th percentile corresponds to which cumulative frequency?
questions.answer: The 80th percentile corresponds to $0.80 \times 200 = 160$ on the vertical cumulative frequency axis.
questions.explanation: The 80th percentile corresponds to $0.80 \times 200 = 160$ on the vertical cumulative frequency axis.

questions.q: Using linear interpolation on grouped data, the median lies in the class $40 \leq x < 50$ with frequency 25 and cumulative frequency before this class equal to 35. If total $n = 100$, find the estimated median.
questions.answer: Median position $= 100/2 = 50$. We need $50 - 35 = 15$ more items out of 25. Median $= 40 + \frac{15}{25}(10) = 40 + 6 = 46.0$.
questions.explanation: Median position $= 100/2 = 50$. We need $50 - 35 = 15$ more items out of 25. Median $= 40 + \frac{15}{25}(10) = 40 + 6 = 46.0$.
